subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister was also given the power to avail himself of such provisions under the munitions and supply act as are required for the carrying out of the duties of the Canadian Commercial Corporation as

the agency. The statements I have read by those who introduced that act have absolutely no meaning, more than that they were insincere and improper and misleading, unless they were intended to convey, and did convey, the impression that the Canadian Commercial Corporation was to be the post-war civilian body set up by this government as the procurement agency for the Department of National Defence.
Having done that, if the government thinks that its powers should be widened, if the government thinks that some of the provisions of the munitions and supply act which are being employed in connection with the activities of the Canadian Commercial Corporation should be widened, then it would be a simple thing to bring in an amendment to the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act. If the government decided that, instead of having two acts, there should be one, it would be possible for them to introduce an amendment to the provisions of the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act, 1939. Then we would have in one act an up to date, effective and understandable piece of legislation dealing with the procurement of the defence requirements of this country.
At this point let me make one thing perfectly clear. The experience and service of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) in war as in peace demonstrate his unusual ability to discuss this whole subject, and what he has said leaves no doubt whatever that we want the most effective, the most efficient and the most up to date procedure that is available for the purpose of giving to our armed forces on land, in the air and at sea the finest type of equipment that human ingenuity and our productive capacity can produce. That is what we have been urging.
When we were urging the Minister of National Defence to tell us what we need under this new agreement which was settled in London only a couple of weeks ago and which the press of the world has hailed as a history-making agreement, we were really asking him to tell us frankly what kind of equipment our forces need. We were asking him to tell us how we could support him in giving to these men in uniform, whether it be khaki, light blue or dark blue, the very best that a great industrial nation could give to them with the backing of parliament which represents the people. That is what we have been asking.
I am only putting this forward in the belief that we should have an act which retains in the hands of parliament those appropriate controls which are the responsibility of parliament in peacetime. This bill
Defence Supplies
should provide legislation which will give the most effective possible productive opportunities in this country to provide those things that we really need, and it should also retain whatever restraints there should be and introduce whatever new restraints there should be so that this cruel demand which has been enforced upon our taxpayers so-shortly after another war for hundreds of millions of dollars for our defence shall not be the means of profiteering now or in the future.
This present bill, far from being restrictive, is the broadest possible piece of legislation imaginable. It is true that it does not say in explicit terms that the minister can force any industry to do anything, but the minister can buy or otherwise acquire, exchange, process, develop, repair, maintain, store and transport defence supplies. He can acquire those things in any way which he himself deems advisable with the support of the government.
Let us see what this bill does and does not do. With the other acts repealed, under this bill no tender need be called for at any time. If hon. members of this house are so gullible as to believe that there is no danger in a provision of that kind, then they have not been following the examination of the public accounts even during the present session. There are no safeguards of any kind which the parliament of Canada, the supreme representative body of the people, could exercise to protect the people's interests.
The board provided by the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act goes. There is to be just one man. Of course that man has the warm and high commendation which has been given to him by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), but even if all of us shared that warm admiration, I still think that with all that admiration-

What I said in regard to the hon. member for Fort William was sincere because I am sure every hon. member loves his warm and genial spirit.. But I am not saying anything offensive when-. I point out that what he has said has in it the very essence of the possibility of dictatorship, although I know he never meant that.

I can remember quite distinctly when those in Germany who were supporting the regime that came into power in January, 1933, said, "We trust this man, we leave it to him." The same thing happened in Italy and they said, "We trust this man, we leave it to him. We do not want any legislation talked about because after all he has done such a good job in building roads and making our trains run on time and no legislation is required." Then in Russia there were people, many of them quite sincere, who said, "This man is doing a good job. He has built a nice subway for us here in Moscow and we do not want any talk about legislation." And so it was in Germany. Instead of debate and discussion they simply said: "Here is the man. Heil Hitler!" In Italy people said: "Here is a man who has done a good job. Viva Duce!" In Russia they said: "Here is a man who has done a good job. Tovarich!" And so it went. Many very bad things resulted from that point of view. It would be most unfortunate indeed if we should forget today that many of the people who supported Hitler and Mussolini-

That is as utterly untrue as other statements that have been made. As a matter of fact, if the hon. member would toother about being a little more accurate and careful he would find that I was one of the first to warn of the danger of the threat of German arms, to urge the rearming of our country, and to try to impress upon this government the necessity of bringing our defence forces up to some state of efficiency. I did that in different articles, and particularly in one which some of the members of the government did not like very much, entitled "Our Bow and Arrow Army". It was written for the purpose of meeting the threat of dictatorship I described which was emerging in Europe at that time. The fact is that those who have seen these things are likely to realize perhaps a little better the extent to which sincere people can be carried away by what they see.
Like everyone else who saw it I pointed out the way that people in those countries were impressed with the efficiency that appeared, with the fact that, as I said before, railways were run better, roads were better, and a lot of other things were better. Anyone who was not blind would have said that, and anyone who reported that was not supporting the regime.

This merely indicates of course the kind of device that is employed at all times to divert attention from the really serious considerations before the house. We are being asked to remove wise restraints that were introduced by this very government at a time when some of its members understood the real and fundamental principles of democracy. We are also being asked to repeal other legislation without even having information as to why some of these things are being done. We are being asked to repeal two acts under the present bill without any explanation why the Canadian Commercial Corporation cannot carry forward the work that it was intended to do. We are also being asked to repeal the existing restraints on profits without any explanation as to why it would not be wise to carry them forward.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) takes very much to heart any suggestion that we should examine these things on the basis of parliamentary practice and established procedure. The fact is that as many free parliaments have been destroyed by sincere men and women doing the wrong thing without realizing that what they were doing was wrong, and really with the hope of improving the efficiency of government, as have been destroyed by force of arms. People forget that in Germany, Italy, Russia and other countries there were many sincere people who really thought that it was worth while to do away with ordinary parliamentary rights so that one man could act quickly without waiting for parliament to approve. Many people who thought that had no sinister motive. Of course many who did and many who supported that form of government had the most sinister motives.
I am not imputing sinister motives of any kind, but I say that the passage of this measure in peacetime, which will be read toy the courts with the knowledge that these emergency powers were conferred in times of peace, without any restraints on profit or any of the other restraints imposed by one of the acts to toe repealed, is opening the door to dictatorship. The only restraint on that is not one that can be exercised by parliament tout is a restraint which will remain in the hands of one man and the government around him.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. The hour is later, and I believe the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) wishes to deal with one or two bills. The threat seems to be made from all sides of the house that this legislation will be defeated. I will say at once it is all right with me if it is defeated because I will at least get full marks for having tried to remove from the statutes legislation that is far too dictatorial and stringent for peacetime. I have tried to retain from the existing legislation only those powers, which are reasonable peacetime powers for carrying out the procurement duties involved in the defence of Canada. Even in peacetime provision for the defence of our country is important business. I believe that the defence of Canada even in peacetime is the most important business carried on in the country. If it is not, certainly the budget is badly distorted, since a considerable part of the taxation levied in this country is being spent on national defence.
We will concede that it is perhaps the most important business of the country. Therefore who can object to its having priority over other business in the matter of procurement? The power of priority is the only arbitrary power retained in the act. True we have taken power to compel a contractor to carry out a contract that he signs of his own volition. In wartime we had the right to go to a factory and say: You must make this. It is needed for defence. You have the facilities and you must make it. We are dropping that power, but if a contractor accepts a contract of his own volition to deliver defence supplies or munitions, then we are taking the power to say that he must carry out the terms of his contract and give his defence contract priority over other contracts he may have taken before or since.
We all know that there is no machinery in most government contracts to compel the contractor to carry out the work on time. We used to include penalty clauses, but I think they have been pretty generally done away with. It may be important, and usually is, in connection with a defence contract that the work be carried out according to the terms of the contract. Therefore we are reserving the right to demand from the contractor priority over contracts that he may have for less essential work. If any material is needed for defence we have power to requisition it. We are being criticized because the power of requisition carries with it the power to fix prices, subject to revision
Defence Supplies by the courts. Well, without the power to fix prices the power to requisition means nothing. Suppose I were to requisition from a stockpile of copper. I suppose copper today is worth about 23 cents a pound, and I say to the owners, "You must deliver it." The owner may reply, "We will deliver it, but the price is 60 cents a pound." That effectively stops the requisitioning from a practical viewpoint. We simply take the position that if we offer the going price of the day the copper must be delivered. If there are any circumstances that have not been taken into account in fixing that price the owner of the copper can go to the exchequer court, present his facts and have his contract revised.
If those are arbitrary powers, then we are taking arbitrary powers. We have those powers today, and of course we have powers that go far beyond them. Today we have the power to order a man to take a contract, to fix the price at which he will carry it out, to renegotiate our agreement at any time, and to revise the price. Today we have all those powers which in my opinion are not peacetime powers. Therefore we are asking that they be rescinded.
Now I come to the point raised by the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) and echoed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), that we should have an arbitrary profit limitation. The difficulty there is in framing limitations that would take account of all the conditions that apply to production. A contract carrying a profit of four per cent in certain industries could make a fortune for the owners. A highly mechanized industry might do very well on a profit of four per cent. An industry that is not mechanized, that depends upon handwork for its production, might be very likely to go broke on a profit of ten per cent. That is a condition of manufacturing. To set up arbitrary legislative limitations that would cover the great range of manufacturing going into the production of munitions, even in peacetime, is a task that I do not think any parliament could undertake and carry out satisfactorily.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: Then what about a tax on excess profits?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
How can we impose a tax that does not apply to all production? Take the Canadian General Electric Company, and I mention this company because it is one of our big corporations, manufacturing a wide range of products. Five per cent of their factory might be devoted to the production of war materials and ninety-five per cent to the production of peacetime materials. How could you apply a tax there? No; we think our best protection is the experience of our

Defence Supplies
purchasing agents in placing contracts with companies at profits that are reasonable.
I suppose it is quite needless to say again that responsibility for the procurement of defence supplies is the responsibility of the minister, not of the corporation. That was the case when the Department of Munitions and Supply Act was passed in 1939. It has been the position ever since, and is the position today. I have heard more kind words in this debate about the Canadian Commercial Corporation than ever before, and I agree with everything that has been said. But I cannot understand the desire to substitute a bureaucracy-for certainly the Canadian Commercial Corporation is a bureaucracy- for a minister who carries his responsibility into this House of Commons. It has always seemed to the government that responsibility for defence purchasing should rest directly upon the shoulders of a minister. That was the position throughout the war, it is the position today, and will continue to be the position under this new legislation.
I do not think I need say much more. Perhaps the house would be interested in the size of the operation we have been discussing. Hon. members may think that defence purchasing does not mean very much in peacetime, but in 1949 the minister was responsible for placing 84,632 separate contracts having a value of $197,445,808.22. In addition there were 19,561 amendments to contracts, resulting in additional expenditures of $24,092,871.37. I just point out that the 104,193 separate transactions for which the minister was responsible represented over 350 transactions per day for the three hundred working days of the year. It is all very well to say that the minister should have no latitude and should obtain the approval of parliament for every separate transaction. I venture to say that parliament and even the government would have some trouble in approving 350 separate transactions every working day in the year. Therefore I think the limitation involved in the review by the government of transactions having to do with defence purchasing is reasonable.
A great deal has been said about this legislation being built around the present minister. Nothing could be more nonsensical. For his sins, the present minister was made minister of munitions and supply throughout the war years, from 1939 to 1946. At the end of that time it seemed that the department had served

its purpose. However, a number of continuing functions had to be carried on, and the minister recommended to the Prime Minister that the responsibility of procurement for the armed services should be turned over to the minister of trade and commerce, who at that time was my colleague Hon. J. A. MacKinnon. It was turned over to him, and I thought that was the last I would see of procurement for the defence services. However, it happened that a few months later Mr. MacKinnon retired from the government, and I was appointed Minister of Trade and Commerce. It was purely a coincidence, and nothing in this legislation would be changed by one iota whoever happened to be minister. The minister has experienced advisers who were through the war with him, in the heads of the Canadian Commercial Corporation. During the war they were members of an organization that purchased over $13 billion worth of munitions and supplies within something like five or six years. I doubt whether anywhere in the world can be found a group with wider experience in purchasing defence materials than is to be found in the Canadian Commercial Corporation, who are the advisers of the Minister of Trade and Commerce of the day, as far as the purchase of defence supplies is concerned.
I have a number of notes here, but if I followed them I am afraid the debate would take rather a frivolous turn. I believe I have stated the facts. If there are those who believe it would be preferable to retain the wartime powers and use them in peacetime instead of those suggested in this legislation, they would be quite justified in voting against this bill. Those who believe we should have a peacetime act for a peacetime period will, I believe, find little justification for voting against this bill.
